core_obligations: Show the easy direction: dominant morphisms are preserved by flat base change, quasi-compactness is fpqc local on the base, and being dominant is Zariski local on the base (proof lines 5842-5847).

In the descent direction, suppose the base change of f along a surjective morphism S' to S is dominant, and note that the composite of the base change with S' to S is dominant as a composite of two dominant morphisms (proof lines 5848-5852).
Identify that composite with the composite of the projection with f, and conclude that f is dominant (proof lines 5852-5853).
Combine with the quasi-compact half to obtain fpqc locality of the conjunction (proof lines 5845-5846).
proof_roadmap: Easy direction: flat base change and Zariski locality (proof lines 5842-5847).
Descent direction: dominance of a composite of dominants (proof lines 5848-5852).
Conclude dominance of the original morphism (proof lines 5852-5853).
difficulty_reason: The lemma asserts that the property of a morphism of being quasi-compact and dominant is fpqc local on the base (statement lines 5835-5838). The proof dispatches the easier direction first: preservation under flat base change is a cited property of dominant morphisms, and quasi-compactness is fpqc local on the base by an earlier lemma of the chapter, while being dominant is Zariski local on the base (proof lines 5842-5847). The descent direction is then proved in full: for a surjective morphism of schemes, flat or not, whose base change of f is dominant, the composite of the base change with the given morphism is dominant as a composite of two dominant morphisms, and since that composite is also the composite of the projection with f, dominance of f follows (proof lines 5848-5853). The claim is H2: the argument is short, but the descent step is genuinely argued rather than cited, and it is worth noting that neither flatness nor quasi-compactness of the given surjective morphism is used there, which is exactly what the author points out in parentheses.
